A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CopyPasteLLM research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original prompting and trained-model evaluations in Tables 1–3, plus copying, relevance, logits, and hidden-state analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds component ablations, subgroup evaluations, response analyses, and training dynamics.

M1.justification: The three prompting procedures, preference construction, answer stamping, DPO objective, and knowledge-capturing procedure are unchanged. All four algorithm bodies match after renumbering. New implementation disclosures and experimental ablation variants do not revise the proposed full method.

E1.justification: Both versions use RAGTruth, FaithEval, PubMedQA, and ConFiQA with the same underlying task coverage. The 20,000-example PubMedQA evaluation already appears in v1 Table 3. v2's knowledge-type, ambiguity, and MeSH breakdowns partition existing coverage; ARC supplies a classification taxonomy, not an additional evaluated benchmark.

E2.justification: External comparator membership in the retained benchmark tables is unchanged. Appendix G and Figure 12 add two evaluated comparison variants, w/o Copying and w/o Stamping, alongside the full model and Base; these are limited additions of ablation controls.

E3.justification: v2 introduces substantial protocols for added analyses: knowledge-type classification and subgroup evaluation, fragment-length relevance analysis, and checkpoint ablations on Llama-3.1-8B over two epochs and 218 steps. The ablations evaluate every 10 steps and introduce JSON-formatted Accuracy after CoT with temperature 0.7 and top-p 0.95. These supplement rather than replace the retained main evaluation and training settings.

E4.justification: New Appendices E–G test performance across knowledge types, biomedical ambiguity and MeSH categories, analyze response length and copied-fragment relevance, and isolate high-copying preference data and answer stamping through ablations. Figure 12 additionally examines convergence and generation stability. v1 lacks these component tests and detailed diagnostic analyses.

E5.justification: v2 adds 95% t-distribution confidence intervals across eight evaluation seeds in Figure 12, five-run majority voting for knowledge-type annotation, and median-plus-standard-deviation reporting in Table 5. These substantially expand statistical reporting beyond v1's point performance estimates and representation visualizations. The eight seeds concern evaluation randomness, not eight independently trained models.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and v1 Table 5, now Table 6, retain their numerical results. v2 nevertheless adds substantial subgroup, response-statistics, and ablation results. For example, its new PubMedQA-Labeled analysis reports Llama-3.1-8B Consensus accuracy of 84.58% versus Attributed's 76.79%, but Negotiation accuracy of 44.93% versus 46.38%. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over corresponding v1 scores.

T1.justification: New Appendix A introduces mathematical arguments connecting copying to contextual attention concentration and conditional-entropy reduction, including Equations 2–7. v1 contains no corresponding derivation. This is substantive new mathematical reasoning, although the asserted attention and entropy relationships are not established through rigorous proofs.

C1.justification: Both versions claim that high-copying prompting and preference training improve contextual faithfulness with 365 training examples, and attribute effectiveness to recalibrated parametric reliance. v2 distinguishes the Copy-Paste paradigm from its CopyPasteLLM implementation more explicitly, but this clarifies ideas already present in v1. The headline performance and efficiency claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds attention-anchoring and entropy explanations, interprets copying as selective evidence use rather than indiscriminate reproduction, and explains answer stamping as enforcing a final commitment. It also connects weak or negative Negotiation-subset gains to ambiguous evidence lacking decisive copyable fragments. The original incomplete-context and future-work limitations are retained through relocation.

D1.justification: v2 discloses previously unspecified prompting details, including extraction validation at 0.95 similarity, LangGraph implementation, five refinement iterations, a 0.99 copying threshold, score coefficients, and temperature 0.1. Table 4 clarifies training-example allocation and PubMedQA sampling. Section 8 now states that implementation is available, replacing its future-release wording; the repository address already appeared in v1's abstract.

R1.justification: v2 adds Clark et al. (2018) for the ARC knowledge taxonomy and Olsson et al. (2022) for induction heads. These support the new analyses and mechanistic interpretation. The main related-work discussion and positioning against existing faithfulness methods remain largely unchanged.

P1.justification: The appendix organization is substantially revised: the standalone formalization section is redistributed into implementation and analysis sections, prompting results receive structured copying and relevance discussions, and limitations and LLM-use disclosures move. Terminology is standardized around Copy-Paste, with revised abstract and conclusion framing. The main section sequence remains stable.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 7–12 and a new Table 5, introducing subgroup charts, fragment-relevance plots, response statistics, and learning curves with confidence bands. Table 4 gains explicit sample allocations. Existing figures are retained with relocation or legend changes, while prompt boxes are substantially compressed through smaller typography.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's missing component validation through copying and stamping ablations, while subgroup results expose an important boundary on ambiguous evidence. Added implementation details and uncertainty reporting make the evidence more assessable and reproducible despite unchanged headline scores. These gains outweigh weaknesses in the additions: Appendix A asserts unproved attention and entropy relationships, and Appendix E.2's claim of matching or beating baselines in every category overstates Figure 7.
